source: Goli & Singh (2024) Can LLMs Capture Human Preferences?
finding: GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 were asked intertemporal choices in 22 languages. Both are far more impatient than humans. Language differences exist but the ranking of languages depends on the elicitation method.
numbers: Larger-later reward chosen 22% (GPT-3.5) and 16% (GPT-4) on average in standard conjoint; 34.5% for GPT-4 with chain-of-thought conjoint. By language: Malay 37.2% (GPT-3.5) and 29% (GPT-4) down to Russian 6.6% and 4.9%.
limits: Rank order of languages changes with method, so language effects are partly a prompt artefact. Pooled discount rates exceed 1, far above human studies.
agent_relevance: Prompt language can shift an LLM's time-preference answers, but chain-of-thought changes results more than language does. Not a clean Whorf test.

source: Goli & Singh (2024) Can LLMs Capture Human Preferences? (future tense test)
finding: Tests the linguistic-savings idea (future tense reference, FTR) in GPT-4. The model is somewhat more patient in weak-FTR languages (German, Mandarin, Japanese and others) than strong-FTR ones.
numbers: Standard conjoint, discount-rate 95% CI weak-FTR [1.715,1.948] vs strong-FTR [1.948,2.210] (they touch at 1.948). Chain-of-thought: [1.206,1.367] vs [1.301,1.470]. 10 of 22 languages are weak FTR.
limits: Intervals nearly overlap. The human linguistic-savings hypothesis itself failed randomised replications (see c24).
agent_relevance: A weak-FTR patience pattern in an LLM may echo the published human correlation in training text. Do not read it as Whorfian thought in the model.

source: Goli & Singh (2024) topic analysis of GPT-4 explanations
finding: Reading the model's own explanations, strong-FTR languages mention risk and uncertainty less often.
numbers: Risk and uncertainty topic discussed 20% less than average in strong-FTR languages; opportunity cost 13.8%; urgency -8.3% (their Table 3 text).
limits: Topic coding of generated text; correlational.
agent_relevance: Shows a method: compare reasoning text across prompt languages, not only final answers.

source: Marjieh et al. (2023) Large language models predict human sensory judgments across six modalities
finding: GPT-3, GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 gave pairwise similarity for colour, pitch, loudness, timbre, taste and consonants. All correlate with human data. The pitch spiral and colour wheel are recovered from text alone.
numbers: Pearson r: pitch .92 (GPT-4, CI .91-.92), loudness .89 (GPT-3.5), colour .89 (GPT-4); consonants .57, taste .54, timbre .42; all models above .6 for the top three domains.
limits: Pitch and consonant human datasets were new, so not in training data. Western listeners only for pitch.
agent_relevance: Text carries much perceptual structure, so language-driven psychophysics can be partly read off a model. Weak for taste and timbre.

source: Marjieh et al. (2023) octave equivalence and cross-lingual colour
finding: Model similarity spikes at 12 semitones (octave) as in human listeners. In English and Russian colour naming, GPT-4 reproduces the Russian split of blue into goluboj (light blue) and sinij (dark blue).
numbers: Dominant-category counts of Munsell chips: sinij 18 (GPT-4) vs 29 (humans); goluboj 33 vs 26. Humans: 103 English and 51 Russian speakers. Agreement with human English naming reported as CI [0.45,0.52] for one model and 0.35 for GPT-3, against a lab ceiling of 0.73-0.75 (Lindsey and Brown).
limits: GPT-4 over-picks turquoise (46 chips vs 15 in humans). Only two languages. The model may echo written descriptions of the Russian blue split.
agent_relevance: Language-specific categories can be recovered by prompting in that language. Closest LLM test of the Russian blue result.

source: Marjieh et al. (2023) GPT-4 vision co-training finding
finding: GPT-4, co-trained on vision and language, did not show gains specific to the visual domain (colour).
numbers: Authors state vision co-training did not necessarily help; no single figure recorded here.
limits: One closed model; mechanism unknown.
agent_relevance: Image grounding may add little beyond language for perceptual similarity.

source: Imel & Zaslavsky (2026) Evolution and compression in LLMs: human-aligned categorization
finding: 39 models in 6 families named colour chips. Larger, instruction-tuned models match English colour naming better and are more efficient (information bottleneck). Iterated in-context learning moves random colour systems toward efficient ones.
numbers: 39 models, 6 families (Gemini, Gemma 3, Llama 3, Qwen 2.5, Olmo 2, GPT-2). Only Gemini 2.0 recovers the wide human complexity range; other frontier models collapse to low-complexity systems. Convergence after roughly 4 generations.
limits: Instruction tuning does not guarantee alignment (Llama 3.3 70B inst. is poor). Some models match low-resource World Color Survey languages, not English.
agent_relevance: Category efficiency is a measurable LLM bias but depends on model strength.

source: Imel & Zaslavsky (2026) input format effect
finding: Showing colours as images instead of sRGB text did not help larger models and sometimes hurt them. Smaller models improved with images. CIELAB coordinates made all models worse.
numbers: Minimal-pair analysis of multimodal LLMs, appendix E; exact deltas not recorded.
limits: Exact deltas not read.
agent_relevance: How a perceptual input is written in the prompt matters. Use the format the model saw most in training.

source: Maharjan & Cangelosi (2026) Vision-Language Model through the lens of Linguistic Relativity
finding: Per a search summary, a contrastive VLM shows language-conditioned colour category boundaries, while a vision-only control shows no categorical shaping.
numbers: No numbers read. PDF text unreadable in this session; only section titles seen.
limits: Unverified details.
agent_relevance: Suggests language-vision alignment, not perception alone, produces the boundary shift.

source: Akbarinia et al. (2024) Exploring the categorical nature of colour perception: insights from artificial networks
finding: Per a search summary, vision networks capture most human categorical colour effects without language.
numbers: About 80% of human categorical data (search summary, not opened).
limits: Snippet only.
agent_relevance: Colour categories may be largely language-independent, limiting Whorf claims for colour.

source: Zhang et al. (2025, ICLR) Do VLMs represent space and how? COMFORT
finding: Nine VLMs tested for spatial frame of reference. Most prefer the English egocentric relative frame with reflected front-back mapping. They fail to switch frames when told to, and robustness is poor.
numbers: Aggregated accuracy under explicit frame prompts 47-63% (GPT-4o 60.3%, XComposer2 63.3%, InstructBLIP 47.2%, near chance). GPT-4o egocentric prompt 78.3%.
limits: Synthetic scenes. Prompts for other languages made with Google Cloud Translate.
agent_relevance: Models default to one spatial frame; naming the frame in the prompt does not reliably fix it.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) COMFORT multilingual test in 109 languages
finding: GPT-4o prompted in 109 languages shows the English relative frame with reflected convention in nearly all. Hausa and Tamil, whose human speakers differ from English, still get the English pattern.
numbers: 109 languages, 170 regions. Konkani, Kurdish and Amharic near random with no preference.
limits: Machine-translated prompts, GPT-4o only.
agent_relevance: Cross-lingual spatial relativity is mostly absent in the model. English habits leak into other languages.

source: Premsri & Kordjamshidi (2025) FoREST: frame of reference evaluation
finding: Text LLMs differ in frame bias. Llama3-70B systematically reverses left and right when converting perspective, unlike English speakers who reverse front and back. Spatial-Guided prompting helps.
numbers: Best frame conversion accuracy 55.5% (Llama3-70B, CoT). GPT-4o relatum-to-camera up to 82.4% with in-context learning, camera-to-relatum 53%. Humans above 90%. Spatial-Guided prompting raised correct-perspective identification by 2.9% to 30% where context and question share a perspective.
limits: No gain where context and question differ in perspective. Llama3 camera questions not helped.
agent_relevance: Extract the frame and primitive relations explicitly before reasoning. It helps identification, not conversion.

source: Cohn & Blackwell (2024) Evaluating LLMs on cardinal directions
finding: Cardinal-direction (absolute frame) reasoning is fine for recall but poor in scenario tasks, even at temperature 0.
numbers: Simple set accuracy above 0.8 for all models; complex templated set best model (gpt-35-turbo-0125) 0.595; only 294 of 5760 questions (5.10%) answered correctly by all models.
limits: Templates with locomotion and person variations; roads and turning backwards hardest.
agent_relevance: Absolute-frame speakers (Guugu Yimithirr) dead-reckon constantly; LLMs lack this without tools.

source: Gurnee & Tegmark (2024) Language models represent space and time
finding: Llama-2 models hold linear internal coordinates for places and for dates, with individual space and time neurons.
numbers: Out-of-sample R2 linear probe, Llama-2-70b: world 0.896, USA 0.825, NYC 0.237, historical figures 0.804, entertainment 0.806, headlines 0.645. Nonlinear MLP adds little.
limits: Probing shows decodability, not use. Space and time are separate probes, not tests of time-as-space metaphors.
agent_relevance: Space and time are linearly readable, so spatial scaffolds for temporal reasoning have a representational basis. Causal use not shown.

source: Wang et al. (2025) Under the Shadow of Babel: BiCause
finding: Tests linguistic relativity in LLMs with bilingual causal-reasoning data. Attention follows typology (Chinese focuses more on causes). Reversed causal order hurts Chinese more.
numbers: Qwen1.5-1.8B: 91.0% (En) vs 91.2% (Zh) forward; reversed chains En 88.5% vs Zh 76.5%. Llama-3.2-3B En 27.0% vs Zh 56.8% in main table. 400 samples in total.
limits: Small dataset (50 samples per cell); attention analysis on one small model.
agent_relevance: Models carry language-specific order habits; test an agent in more than one prompt language when order matters.

source: Wang et al. (2025) BiCause scale effect
finding: Larger Qwen models show small English-Chinese gaps.
numbers: Qwen1.5-14B En 96.8 vs Zh 96.0; 72B En 95.5 vs Zh 92.2; 32B En 92.8 vs Zh 91.8.
limits: Gaps small and not consistent in direction.
agent_relevance: Language effects on reasoning shrink with scale.

source: Alper & Averbuch-Elor (2023) Kiki or Bouba? Sound symbolism in vision-and-language models
finding: CLIP and Stable Diffusion show the sound-shape (bouba/kiki) association by zero-shot probing.
numbers: Stable Diffusion AUC 0.74, accuracy 80%; CLIP AUC 0.77, 52%. Humans: 89% success kiki/bouba, 78% on random pseudowords.
limits: Sound-shape, not time, space or pitch. Adjacent paradigm.
agent_relevance: Non-arbitrary sound-meaning ties exist in text-image models.

source: Verhoef, Shahrasbi & Kouwenhoven (2024) What does Kiki look like?
finding: Four VLMs tested; evidence for a bouba-kiki effect is limited. Only CLIP and GPT-4o go in the right direction in some tests.
numbers: Jagged vs curved: CLIP b = -1.79 (CI -3.86 to -0.05), GPT-4o b = -3.51 (CI -6.69 to -1.37). Humans about 95% pick jagged for kiki.
limits: Few trials; different pseudowords from Alper et al. BLIP2 and ViLT not conclusive.
agent_relevance: Partial failure to replicate: iconicity effects depend on model and method.

source: Loakman, Li & Lin (2024) With Ears to See and Eyes to Hear
finding: LLMs and VLMs on sound symbolism. Agreement with humans varies widely; extra task information in the prompt sometimes helps and sometimes hurts. Magnitude symbolism is easier than shape.
numbers: Iconicity rating Spearman vs humans: GPT-4 .537 (Nov 2023) vs .575 (Trott 2024); GPT-3.5 .420; LLaMA-2 70B .304; Mistral-7B .382; FLAN-T5 about 0.
limits: Compares to majority-vote human labels, ignoring individual differences.
agent_relevance: Prompt variants change results a lot. Report them.

source: Zhao (2026) Evidence for systematic semantic structure in individual letters
finding: GPT-4o, Claude Sonnet 4 and Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite rated 8,714 nonwords on nine dimensions including elevation and weight. Preregistered human tests (N=1,388) confirmed the model-derived profiles.
numbers: Model reliability corrected r 0.79 (temperature) to 0.92 (weight). Native English readers 85.3% (selected items), 65.7% (all contrasts); five other languages 76.7% and 68.4%.
limits: Preprint. Temperature was the weakest dimension.
agent_relevance: LLM-generated cross-modal hypotheses can be human-validated: a model-as-hypothesis-generator pipeline.

source: Illan Castillo & Valenzuela (2025) Using AI to replicate human experimental results: a motion study
finding: GPT-4 replicated four human psycholinguistic studies on manner-of-motion verbs in temporal expressions, using the same instructions as the human participants.
numbers: Spearman between .73 and .96 across studies (.73 for the first rating study, .96 for valence).
limits: Spanish motion-verb stimuli, one model. Not an ego-moving or time-moving test.
agent_relevance: Cheap in-silico replication works if the human instructions are reused verbatim.

source: Cultural interpretability framework (2024) Toward cultural interpretability
finding: Conceptual paper. Lists linguistic relativity (grammar shaping concepts of space, time and more) as one of three research axes for describing LLMs.
numbers: No experiments.
limits: Position paper, no data.
agent_relevance: Motivates per-language testing of agents but gives no method.

source: Chen, He & Riyanto (2019) and Angerer (2025) randomised tests of the linguistic-savings hypothesis
finding: Per search summaries, randomly assigning future or present tense wording gave no causal effect on patience.
numbers: Austrian replication 332 subjects (search summary, not opened).
limits: Snippet only.
agent_relevance: Supports reading LLM FTR patterns as data artefacts rather than causal Whorf effects.

source: Dolscheid et al. (2014) Dutch vs Farsi pitch space
finding: Human anchor: Dutch (height words for pitch) and Farsi (thickness words) speakers differ in pitch reproduction under height and thickness interference.
numbers: No numbers read this session.
limits: Snippet only. No LLM version found.
agent_relevance: No LLM replication of the height versus thickness pitch metaphor was found.

source: Search gap note: LLM tests of ego-moving vs time-moving and horizontal/vertical time metaphors
finding: No paper testing LLMs on spatial time metaphors (ego-moving, time-moving, vertical Mandarin time) or on the pitch height versus thickness metaphor turned up. OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar and arXiv API were rate-limited this session, so coverage is partial.
numbers: 0 direct studies found in 9 web searches.
limits: Absence of evidence under limited search.
agent_relevance: Open gap. A cheap ego-moving and time-moving prompt probe of the agent's model would be new.
